pages.x: When the Prophet Muhammad died in 632, most of Arabia had accepted Islam. The first caliph, Abu Bakr, put down the tribes that broke away, then sent armies north against the two great powers of the day, Rome and Persia, both worn out by a long war with each other and by plague.

The most famous Arab general, Khalid ibn al-Walid, called the Sword of God, led his men on a daring march across the Syrian desert. In 636, by the river Yarmouk, the Arabs destroyed a great Roman army, and Syria was lost to Rome for good.

At about the same time, at Qadisiyyah in Iraq, an Arab army beat the Persians after days of fighting, war elephants and all. The Persian capital Ctesiphon fell with its treasures. By 651 the last Persian king was dead and his empire gone.

Under the second caliph, Umar, the Arabs took Jerusalem in 637 or 638. Tradition says Umar came in person, dressed simply, and promised the Christians safety for their lives, their property and their churches. Egypt fell soon after.

The Arab armies were small, but united by their new faith and well led, and their enemies were exhausted. Many conquered peoples did not resist. They paid a tax and kept their own religions, and only slowly, over centuries, did most of them become Muslim.

The Umayyad caliphs, ruling from Damascus, pushed on across North Africa. In 711 Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed to Spain with Berber and Arab troops, and the rock where he landed was named after him: Jabal Tariq, Gibraltar. In a few years almost all of Spain was theirs.

In 732 a Frankish army under Charles Martel beat an Arab raiding army between Tours and Poitiers. In the east, Arab armies had reached the Indus and Central Asia. By 750 the caliphate ran from the Atlantic to the borders of India and China.

The conquests were matched by civil wars over who should lead the Muslims, which left the lasting split between Sunni and Shia. In 750 the Abbasid family overthrew the Umayyads and moved the capital east, soon to their new city of Baghdad.

In barely a century the conquests made Arabic the language of the Middle East and North Africa and began the spread of Islam, today the faith of nearly two billion people. The caliphate became one great world of trade and learning, from Spain to Central Asia.
pts: From Arabia to Spain and the Indus in a century
